records.quote:
Lizzie says we were just on the edge of
the new age. It certainly is different. And of course I wouldn't go back
to it for anything.
records.paraphrase: A character contrasts the old-fashioned way of life with the changed present day.

records.quote:
"Maids? Maids? It used to be 'help,'" he had protested. "You don't mean
to say they have waitresses in Binghamville now?"
records.paraphrase: A returning character contrasts older terms and customs with present-day social arrangements in the town.

records.quote:
He winced. His associates were not accustomed to be so scrupulously
accurate. It seemed indecently long ago.
records.paraphrase: Varian reacts uncomfortably to the frank reminder of how much time has passed.

records.quote:
But at her age mother was broken down and
old. She had to be. There were nine of us, and here there's only little
Dudley
records.paraphrase: A character contrasts her mother's worn-out state at a given age with her sister's youthful appearance now.

records.quote:
my mother
went to singing-school, and Lizzie was looking that up in a book, the
other day, to see what they did--she wanted it for a party!
records.paraphrase: A once-ordinary past custom has become a quaint curiosity researched for a party.

records.quote:
Something in the calm sun-bathed
picture tugged strongly at his heart. He thought suddenly of his mother
and his Aunt Delia
records.paraphrase: Varian is emotionally moved by the domestic scene, recalling his mother and aunt.

records.quote:
We've
moved on since you left us, you know.
records.paraphrase: A character notes that the community has changed since another left thirty years earlier.

records.quote:
your view of Binghamville must be
like the old maps of Africa in the green geography, that said 'desert'
and 'interior' and 'savage tribes' from time to time
records.paraphrase: A character contrasts an outdated mental image of the town with how it has changed over time.

criteria.rationale: The story is a domestic social-realist romance set in a contemporary country estate; no scientific facts, theories, discoveries, or natural processes are materially represented.
Only ordinary contemporary objects (phaeton, tea things, golf clubs) appear; no engineered system or invention materially affects the setting, problem, or outcome.

References to change over thirty years and an 'old-fashioned' past are ordinary generational nostalgia within a contemporary present, not a speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement. The 'new age' remark is figurative social commentary.
The story observes social change between generations but does not develop speculative consequences from an identifiable premise; it is nostalgic contrast rather than systematic extrapolation.
No observation, hypothesis, testing, measurement, or systematic evidential reasoning materially drives understanding or action; the plot turns on personal recognition and courtship.
The setting is an ordinary American country estate; there are no other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them.

No large-scale natural, technological, cosmic, biological, or human-caused disaster is actual, impending, remembered, or causally central; only minor personal misfortunes (a fainting, a child's death) appear.

candidates.description: A claimed generational transformation of American social life ('the new age'), in which a formerly toiling farm-woman class of women (like the narrator's mother and Aunt Delia) has been superseded by leisured, ageless, servant-supported women epitomized by Mrs. Dud. The story frames a contrast between an 'old-fashioned' domestic labor order and a modern order.

novelty.rationale: The 'change' described is ordinary generational social change (servants, dressmakers, tutors, leisure) between roughly 1870 and 1900, entirely within the author's empirical world. It is nostalgic realist commentary, not a totalizing or world-altering difference from the empirical norm. Nothing estranges the story universe from the reader's own.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The social order presented is coherent and immanent, grounded in an intelligible account of changing domestic economy and class. It is nonsupernatural and systematic, but this coherence is that of ordinary realism.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The contrast between old and new modes of womanhood does organize the story's central theme and Varian's choice between the two sisters. However, hegemony over an ordinary (non-novel) contrast does not confer novum status.

estrangement.rationale: The reader-facing contrasts (maids vs. help, singing-school as curiosity, mother worn out vs. sister youthful) are nostalgic period contrasts within a mundane realist setting, not cognitive estrangement from an empirical norm.
